extracted.intended_audience: prospective grantees, foundation grant investigators, and philanthropic program officers
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and process guidance used by a foundation (Open Philanthropy / Coefficient Giving) to select, evaluate, approve, and monitor grants, including cause-selection heuristics, evaluation questions, and operational practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grant Investigation (stage)
rubrics_metrics.description: During investigation, an Open Philanthropy investigator works with a potential grantee to explore and develop a funding proposal by discussing proposed activities, budget, anticipated challenges, and desired outcomes of the project.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigator engages iteratively with potential grantee to clarify proposed activities, examine budget realism, surface anticipated challenges, and define desired outcomes before moving to conditional approval. This stage is formative and collaborative rather than a one-shot application review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditional Approval (stage)
rubrics_metrics.description: A formal stage in the four-stage grant process following investigation and preceding formal approval.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed as a standard stage; page does not provide detailed scoring guidance here but positions it as an intermediate approval step between investigation and formal approval.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal Approval (stage)
rubrics_metrics.description: The stage in which a grant receives final sign-off and funding is committed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard final decision step after conditions (if any) are resolved; no further procedural detail on the page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation and Close (stage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Post-award stage in which outcomes are evaluated and the grant is closed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes monitoring, evaluation, and acknowledging lessons learned; part of lifecycle to assess whether outcomes were achieved and to capture learning for public reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cause Selection — Importance
rubrics_metrics.description: How many individuals are affected by the problem, and how deeply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a primary axis for choosing causes: high importance means interventions can affect many people or affect them deeply; this drives priority when comparing causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cause Selection — Tractability
rubrics_metrics.description: The likelihood that a philanthropic funder can contribute to significant progress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluates how feasible it is that funding will move the needle on the problem; includes consideration of available interventions, realistic timelines, and leverageability of philanthropic capital.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cause Selection — Neglectedness
rubrics_metrics.description: Causes that receive less attention from others — including donors, businesses, and governments — where each dollar tends to go even further.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize areas where marginal funding has larger marginal impact due to low prior investment by others; used in cross-cause comparisons to find high-leverage opportunities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost-Effectiveness Estimation (BOTEC)
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigators sometimes include a 'back-of-the-envelope-calculation' (BOTEC) to roughly estimate the expected cost-effectiveness of the potential grant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BOTECs are rough quantitative estimates used to compare expected impact per dollar across opportunities; not a formal econometric model but a heuristic to inform comparisons and decisions. Open sharing of cost-effectiveness models is part of transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counterfactual Reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment of what would happen without the grant and whether the grantee is the right partner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific bullets: consider whether it is the best organization to do this work; whether the work is the most valuable use of that organization's additional resources; and what would happen without the grant. Counterfactual analysis is central to judging marginal impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Case-for-Grant: 'What's the case for the grant?'
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicit articulation of the rationale for funding this particular proposal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grant proposals and investigator write-ups should state the case succinctly: why fund this project, what will it achieve, and how does it compare to alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'What's our cost-effectiveness estimate?' (evaluation question)
rubrics_metrics.description: A specific question Open Philanthropy asks to quantify expected impact per dollar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expectations: provide a cost-effectiveness estimate (BOTEC or similar) and explain assumptions and uncertainty; used to compare across differing causes and programs.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Who else is funding this work?' (additionality/landscape)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment of other funders and funding landscape relevant to the proposed work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to judge neglectedness and additionality; helps determine whether marginal funding will be high-impact or merely duplicative.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'What's our counterfactual impact?' (evaluation question)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate the marginal effect of providing the grant versus the next-best alternative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Closely tied to counterfactual reasoning: requires explicit consideration of what would happen absent the grant and whether funds shift outcomes relative to baseline.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'What are the risks?' (risk assessment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identification and analysis of key risks to success, including programmatic, operational, and reputational risks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grant write-ups should discuss plausible failure modes, mitigation strategies, and tolerance for high-risk/high-reward projects (the foundation states comfort with low success rates when expected value is high).

rubrics_metrics.name: 'What's our plan for monitoring and evaluation?' (M&E)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plan for how the foundation and grantee will monitor progress and evaluate outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect explicit M&E plans: metrics, milestones, data collection approaches, reporting cadence. Plans inform both conditional approval terms and later evaluation and close.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'How will we know if this worked?' (outcome measurement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specification of success criteria and evidence that would demonstrate impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires defining measurable indicators or plausible qualitative evidence of success; should inform monitoring and final evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority Focus Area — Global Health and Wellbeing
rubrics_metrics.description: A primary focus area which includes global health, scientific research (esp. for the global south), global development, and farm animal welfare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Projects addressing these topics are core priorities; proposals should align to these domains to be competitive within this focus area.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority Focus Area — Longtermism / Existential Risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Priority focus area including AI risks (alignment, governance), biosecurity and pandemic preparedness, and other potential catastrophic risks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open to funding work aimed at reducing long-term/existential risks, including technical alignment research, governance interventions, and biosafety preparedness. Willingness to fund early-stage and high-uncertainty work in these areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public Reasoning and Transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Detailed grant write-ups published; reasoning made transparent; cost-effectiveness models shared; mistakes acknowledged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open Philanthropy emphasizes publishing reasoning for grants and sharing models and lessons, including acknowledging errors. Transparency is a normative feature of their grantmaking approach and an implicit expectation for grantee reporting in many cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective Altruism Framework / Quantitative, Cause-Neutral Comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: Grew out of the effective altruism community; uses a quantitative/explicit approach to philanthropy and cause-neutral comparisons across very different areas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decision-making favors explicit, often quantitative comparisons of marginal value across causes rather than traditional categorical funding silos; applicants should expect cross-cause trade-offs to be considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Willingness to Make Long-Term, High-Uncertainty Bets
rubrics_metrics.description: Funds high-uncertainty, high-potential-payoff work and is comfortable with low success rates if expected value is high; willing to fund early, exploratory work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foundation tolerates higher probability of failure when the expected upside is large; applicants proposing exploratory or early-stage interventions should clearly articulate expected-value logic and acceptable failure modes.

rubrics_metrics.name: RFP and Sourcing Approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Most grants made to invited applicants; some open Requests for Proposals; active in seeking out promising researchers; often funds new fields/topics that mainstream funders ignore.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants should note that many opportunities are by invitation; proactive outreach, scoping by investigators, and targeted RFPs are common. Novel or underfunded topics may be especially attractive if they score well on cause-selection criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grant Size Categories and Typical Ranges
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical grant size buckets: Small exploratory $50K–$500K; Standard $500K–$5M; Strategic $5M–$50M; Transformative $50M+ (rare).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Size expectations inform realism of proposals and appropriate scope; investigators and applicants should align proposed budgets to these customary ranges and justify departures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduced Reliance on Traditional Peer Review
rubrics_metrics.description: Less reliance on traditional peer review compared to many funders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decision-making can rely more on internal investigator judgment, cost-effectiveness reasoning, and targeted expert input rather than conventional peer-review panels; applicants should present clear causal logic and evidence rather than relying solely on peer-review credentials.
